Lecture 6 Conditional Probability, Independence, the Multiplication Rule and Tree Diagrams

Conditional probability on a two-dice grid, what it means for events to be independent and how to check it, the general multiplication rule for two or more events, tree diagrams, and sampling without replacement with the 5% rule.

3Independent events

Definition

We will say that two events are independent if knowing that one event has or has not occurred does not affect the probability that the other has or has not occurred.

✱ In the previous example, and are not independent. Events and are.

Can we claim this by only knowing that ?

✎ Explanation (added)

The definition asks for a lot: it mentions occurred or not occurred for both events. So far only one of those facts has been checked for and . The next boards show that one check is enough.

Textbook · Devore — independence: Definition in §2.5, p. 85. Devore takes P(A | B) = P(A) as the definition, the first statement on the board.

Moving away from the previous example, let’s consider two arbitrary events and .

Theorem A and B are independent if the following are true
Typed note included in the PDF Every line on the board, in plain words

Setup: “Two arbitrary events A and B” means this now applies to any two events, not just the dice.

Claim: A and B are independent if the following are true (and if one is true, all are).

Left column: learning about B doesn’t change A

EquationMeaning
Learning B happened doesn’t change the chance of A
Learning B didn’t happen doesn’t change the chance of A
Learning B happened doesn’t change the chance of not A
Learning B didn’t happen doesn’t change the chance of not A

Right column: learning about A doesn’t change B

EquationMeaning
Learning A happened doesn’t change the chance of B
Learning A didn’t happen doesn’t change the chance of B
Learning A happened doesn’t change the chance of not B
Learning A didn’t happen doesn’t change the chance of not B

As long as we are in the case where we have nonzero probabilities, if any one of these is true, then they are all true.

If any is false, all are false.

4How to check for independence

Many people use the following to check for independence.

Theorem

⊛ If and , then and are independent provided any one of the following is true.

If any one is true, and are independent.

If any one is false, then and are dependent.

✎ Explanation (added)

In practice, pick whichever check uses the numbers you were given. If you know , and , use (3): multiply and compare. Dice check with (3): , so and are independent; but , so and are dependent.

Do not confuse independent with disjoint (mutually exclusive). Disjoint events with non-zero probabilities are never independent: if one happens, the other certainly did not, which is a big change in its probability.

Textbook · Devore — check (3), A and B are independent if and only if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B): Proposition in §2.5, p. 86, Equation (2.8). Example 2.33 (p. 86) shows that mutually exclusive events with positive probability are dependent.

The Multiplication Rule

✎ Explanation (added)

Both versions come from multiplying a conditional probability formula by its denominator. In words: the probability that both happen the probability the first happens the probability the second happens given that the first did. Use whichever order matches the story (usually the order things happen in time).

Textbook · Devore — the multiplication rule, P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) · P(B): §2.4, p. 77.

The order doesn’t matter, since it’s multiplication.

Pattern: each new event is conditioned on all the events before it. Same idea as each deeper level of a tree.

Textbook · Devore — three events, P(A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ A₃) = P(A₃ | A₁ ∩ A₂) · P(A₂ | A₁) · P(A₁): §2.4, p. 78, Equation (2.4).

If the events are mutually independent, then we get the following multiplication rules for many events.

✎ Explanation (added)

There is really only one multiplication rule, . Independence is the special case where the conditional probability is the same as the plain one, so the bar can be dropped. “And” means multiply, but you may only multiply the plain probabilities when the events are independent. Otherwise the later factors must be conditional.

Mutually independent means that knowing about any combination of the other events does not change the probability of any one of them, which is what allows to be replaced by .

Textbook · Devore — mutually independent events: Definition in §2.5, p. 88.

6Example: rolling a die three times, with tree diagrams

Example

Suppose you roll a fair 6-sided die 3 times.

Let be the event you roll a one on the first roll,

let be the event you roll a one on the second roll,

and let be the event the roll a one on the third roll.

What is the probability you roll three ones?   What is ?

The outcome of any roll is completely unaffected by what happened on any of the other rolls so the events are mutually independent.

We can use tree diagrams to answer questions like this.

Probability we end up here

← Product of the probability labels on the edges we traverse as we move from the top to this node.

A small underlined label at the top left of this board appears to read “Two dice”.

✎ Explanation (added)

A tree is the multiplication rule drawn as a picture. Each node is “what has happened so far”, and each edge carries the probability of the next thing given everything above it. So the edge labels are conditional probabilities, and multiplying down a path is exactly . At every node the edges leaving it must add to 1 (here ).

Textbook · Devore — tree diagrams with a conditional probability on each branch: Example 2.29 and Figure 2.10, pp. 78–79; used together with independence, Example 2.35 and Figure 2.13, p. 87.

(written under the far-left leaf, with an arrow to it)

A small underlined label at the top left of this board looks like “3 coins”; the tree itself is for the 3 rolls of the die. On the left the board also labels the first three left-hand edges P(A), P(B | A) and P(C | A ∩ B).

Note that the events of ending up at different nodes at the bottom are mutually exclusive events.

We get to use the easy version of the addition rule (don’t need to subtract the probability of an intersection).

✎ Explanation (added)

You can only end at one leaf, so two different leaves can never both happen: they are disjoint. That means the probability of “this leaf or that leaf” is a plain sum, with no overlap to subtract. All eight leaf probabilities add to 1: 1 + 5 + 5 + 25 + 5 + 25 + 25 + 125 = 216.

7Example: the probability of rolling two ones

Example
Rule Tree diagram
  1. Locate the nodes you care about.
  2. For each node, multiply the probability labels together on the path to that node.
  3. Add the results.
✎ Explanation (added)

“Two ones” here means exactly two, so the one roll that is not a one can be the third, the second or the first: three different paths. Each path has two factors of and one factor of in some order, so each is , and .

The recipe is the two rules together: multiply along a path (multiplication rule), add across paths (addition rule for mutually exclusive events).

8Sampling without replacement and the 5% rule

Example

241 of the 1000 clerical staff members are men and the remaining 759 are women.

If you choose 2 staff members at random without replacement and all staff members are equally likely to be chosen, what is the probability you choose 1 man and 1 woman?

Tree diagram:

✎ Explanation (added)

“Without replacement” means the first person is not put back, so the second pick is from 999 people and its probabilities depend on the first pick. If a man was chosen first, 240 men and 759 women remain: and . If a woman was chosen first, 241 men and 758 women remain. These second-level numbers are conditional probabilities, and the two picks are dependent.

“1 man and 1 woman” can happen in two orders, man then woman or woman then man, so two leaves are added. Each product is , and twice that is .

Textbook · Devore — sampling without replacement from a small group, with fractions that change after each draw: Example 2.27, p. 78.

Rule

As long as the sample size is relatively small in comparison to the population size, if we are sampling without replacement, we can pretend we are sampling with replacement and get good estimates to probabilities.

Let’s do this for the previous example. (As long as the sample size is no more than 5% of the population size, we will view this as okay)

Typed note included in the PDF The 5% Rule

What he’s saying

Sampling without replacement is exact, but the fractions keep changing.

Sampling with replacement is easier: every pick has the same probability, and the picks are independent.

Rule: if the sample is small compared to the population, you can pretend it’s with replacement, and the answer will be very close.

“Small” means 5% or less

Here = sample size and = population size.

This example: ,

So it’s okay to treat the picks as independent.

Applying it to the staff example

EventExact (without)Estimate (with)
Both men
Both women
One of each

They differ only in the 4th decimal place. The estimate is very good.

The exact answer, , is written above it on the board for comparison.

Try it — when is “pretend it is with replacement” a good estimate?

Keep the same mix (24.1% men) but shrink the population. The sample is always 2 people. Watch the gap between the exact answer and the estimate as the sample becomes a bigger fraction of the population.

Interactive widget: open the page on a screen to use it.
✎ Explanation (added)

Why it works: taking one person out of 1000 hardly changes the mix, so is almost the same as . With replacement the two picks are independent, the tree has the same numbers on every level, and the calculation becomes . The exact value is , a difference of about .

The trade is a tiny loss of accuracy for a much simpler model (independent, identical picks). This is the justification, later in the course, for using the binomial distribution when sampling from a large population.

Try it first, then open the worked answer

Use the 36-square grid from this lecture. (one row), (one column), (the diagonal of 7s).

Pairs. is the single square (red 3, green 4): . : red is 3 and the total is 7, which forces green 4, the same single square: . : green 4 and total 7 forces red 3: . Each time , so by check (3) every pair is independent. The events are pairwise independent.

All three. is again that one square, so . But . These are not equal, so the events are not mutually independent.

Why: once you know and both happened (red 3, green 4), the total is certainly 7, so , not . Knowing one of the others tells you nothing about , but knowing both tells you everything. This is why the definition of mutual independence (Devore p. 88) asks for the product rule for every subset, not just for pairs.

10Lecture at a glance

Conditional probability
Restricting the sample space

“Given ”: keep only the outcomes in and count inside it (classical case).

Independent events

Knowing whether one occurred does not change the probability of the other.

Three checks

One true: independent. One false: dependent.

General multiplication rule
Three events
Mutually independent events
Tree diagrams

Locate the leaves you want. Multiply along each path. Add the results.

5% rule

Then sampling without replacement can be treated as with replacement.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Two dice (or a similar grid of equally likely outcomes): find , , and , by the formula or by restricting the sample space.
  • Decide whether two events are independent, showing which of the three checks you used and what the numbers were.
  • Given , and : fill in a Venn diagram, check independence with , and compute a conditional probability such as .
  • Derive the multiplication rule from the conditional probability formula, or show that implies .
  • A repeated independent experiment (three rolls): draw the tree, and find the probability of “all three” and of “exactly two” by multiplying along paths and adding.
  • Sampling without replacement: draw the tree with the changing fractions and find “one of each”; then say whether the 5% rule allows the with-replacement estimate, and compute it.
